title: Open his eyes (2 Kings 6:15–17)
hookLine: Elisha prays his servant will see the unseen help around them

cards: Dawn in the town of Dothan. The servant of Elisha gets up early, steps out, and stops. An army has surrounded the city in the night: horses, chariots, a great host.

The king of Aram has been at war with Israel, and not once nor twice, the text says, Elisha has warned the king of Israel where the ambush is. So the king of Aram has sent a whole army to capture one prophet.
The servant runs back inside, in pure panic: "Alas, my master! how shall we do?"

teach.b: Elisha's answer is calm, and at first it sounds impossible: "Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them." More? The servant can see an army outside, and on his side, one prophet.
Elisha doesn't argue or explain. He prays one short line: "LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see."
He doesn't ask for the army to disappear, or for rescue, or for fire from heaven. He asks for his servant to see.

And the Lord opened the young man's eyes, "and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha." The help had been there the whole time. Nothing outside changed; the servant did.
Not long before, a chariot of fire parted Elijah from his student. Now chariots of fire surround that student, and Elisha knew it before anyone saw them. Then a surprising turn.
Elisha prays that the enemy soldiers be struck with blindness, and leads them, confused, right into Samaria, to the king of Israel. Shall I strike them? the king asks.

Elisha says no: set bread and water before them, let them eat and drink, and send them home. And the raiding bands of Aram came no more into the land of Israel. So the chapter is about two kinds of sight.
The servant learns to see help he couldn't see. Israel's king is asked to see enemies as hungry men who could be fed. In both, the first change happens in someone's eyes.

how: Jews read the story of Elisha at Dothan as part of the book of Kings; Elisha's line that those with us are more than those with them is remembered as words of courage in frightening times.

games.q: you're Elisha. your servant is terrified: an army surrounds the town. what do you pray for?
o: that you both escape in the night.
that your servant's eyes be opened.
games.why: Elisha prays, open his eyes, that he may see, and the servant sees the mountain full of chariots of fire.

practice: Start with whatever feels like an army around your city today, a deadline, a worry, a stretch of loneliness, and feel how big it is.

Then, like the servant, look again at what's already around you: the chair holding you up, water you can drink, the light you're sitting in, a name in your phone you could call, each one coming into view like horses on a hillside.

wordCard.voice: Elisha, who prayed not for the army to vanish but for his frightened servant's eyes to open, and see the mountain full of chariots of fire.
